approachQuestion.prompt:
Platform route

Positions 0 through n-1 form a route. From position i, you may move forward by any integer distance from 1 through jump[i]. You start at 0. Return whether the last position is reachable; encode true as 1 and false as 0.

Example 1: jump=[2,0,1,0] → 1 using 0→2→3.
Example 2: jump=[1,0,2] → 0.
Example 3: jump=[0] → 1.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 0 ≤ jump[i] ≤ 200000; moves beyond the final position need not be taken. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Maintain farthest, initially 0. Scan positions while i ≤ farthest, extending farthest to max(farthest,i+jump[i]). Return 1 if farthest reaches n-1, and 0 if the scan hits a gap.
options.feedback: Reachable positions form a prefix: every shorter forward move is allowed. Each scanned reachable position extends exactly that prefix; a position beyond it cannot be reached from any processed position.

options.text: Always jump the maximum permitted distance, clamping to the last position.
options.feedback: Committing to a landing can lose a useful intermediate platform. For [2,2,0,0], landing on 2 gets stuck while 0→1→3 succeeds.

options.text: Return 0 whenever any jump entry is zero, unless it is the last entry.
options.feedback: Unreachable or avoidable zero entries do not block the whole route. For [2,0,0], position 0 can jump straight to the end.

options.text: Mark every reachable position in a Boolean array. Process positions in order; from each reachable i, mark every allowed destination individually.
options.feedback: This correctly computes reachability for the entire domain, but repeatedly marks destinations already known to be reachable. One farthest boundary replaces the array and repeated range marking.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above as iterative scans with scalar indices, counters and accumulators. Do not copy the input and do not store a decision list. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: Scan each reachable index once while maintaining a scalar frontier.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: The scan visits each reachable position at most once; an input reaching the final position can require n visits. Updating farthest uses constant work per visit. No route or predecessor array is retained, so auxiliary space is O(1).
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
